title: 1.1 Chapter introduction
text: I am an AI-first technical writer and subject matter expert who turns complex technology into practical guidance. My background in enterprise support and network systems informs how I research product behaviour, write structured documentation, and build tools for research, review, migration, and publishing. My formal role is Technical Writer II at SOTI.

title: 1.2 Who I am
text: I am Aiman Nabeel Peerji, an AI-first technical writer and subject matter expert with a foundation in network systems and enterprise technical support. I investigate how technology works, turn that understanding into usable guidance, and improve the tools and workflows that help teams produce reliable documentation. My current role is Technical Writer II at SOTI. The experience behind this portfolio spans troubleshooting, structured authoring, product research, documentation quality, and AI-assisted automation. My journey began with network-systems education and service desk work at RWDI. Working with directory services, email, computers, and access problems taught me to connect technical details with the person trying to get something done. Enterprise support expanded that experience into device management, identity integration, logs, databases, and customer environments. Writing grew naturally out of that work. Through knowledge-base articles and Project Sherpa, I helped turn individual investigations into reusable knowledge and supported other agents in explaining their findings. Moving into technical writing brought that practice into DITA/XML, source control, peer review, and product releases. Over time, my scope expanded again: from improving individual topics to improving how content is researched, reviewed, migrated, and published. That progression is the central story of this portfolio. SOTI products provide substantial examples of the work. The capabilities I have developed—technical investigation, clear explanation, editorial judgement, collaboration, and practical automation—define my professional direction.

title: 1.3 How I use subject matter expertise
text: My subject matter expertise is grounded in enterprise mobility, device enrollment, identity and directory integration, server behaviour, application deployment, and troubleshooting. As a writer, I use that operational background to ask better questions, investigate prerequisites and exceptions, and check procedures against product evidence. My research includes Signal properties and events, device audit logging, Apple enrollment, and declarative application policies. I also consider the reader's route through the information. Task structure, navigation, screenshots, related guidance, and rendered output all affect whether someone can find and follow an explanation. The writing examples show how I improved those parts of the help.

title: 1.4 What AI-first means in my work
text: I use AI as a regular part of research, drafting, review, and tool development. My work includes reusable documentation skills, workflows that connect product evidence to structured content, and experiments that make authoring and review more accessible. My authoring workflow connects Jira research, implementation details, design evidence, screenshots, DITA source, validation, Git, and peer review. Technical understanding and human judgement remain central to that process. I check generated material, refine review guidance from actual decisions, and distinguish a proposal, a working utility, and a published result. My AI-first approach builds on earlier writing and support experience. The career journey explains how that approach developed. The Projects page follows the tools and workflows, Writing shows inspectable source changes, and Skills pairs the products and tools with the roles where I used them.

title: 2.1 Learning systems through service desk work
text: I began in Service Desk Support at RWDI in Guelph, completing a co-op from January to September 2021 and continuing on a part-time contract from September to December 2021. The role involved both systems administration and direct device support. I used graphical interfaces and PowerShell for Active Directory work, managed DHCP, DNS, and print services, supported user access and remote administration, and performed registry backup and recovery. Exchange Server 2019 and Outlook work included installation and configuration, mailbox delegation, mail flow, shared mailboxes, contacts, distribution lists, permissions, email rules, archiving, recovery, and spam controls. For customers and colleagues, that meant solving the access, mail, network, and device problems that interrupted daily work. The Skills page connects each named system with this role and distinguishes hands-on duties from resume-listed familiarity. I also handled inventory and purchase orders, re-imaged computers, upgraded RAM, network cards, and SSDs, arranged desk setups and manufacturer repairs, and supported network printers. I configured MFA and OneDrive on company phones and supported civil-engineering software such as Sensr and Senseview.

title: 2.2 Entering SOTI Technical Support
text: I joined SOTI in January 2022 in Level 1 Technical Support and progressed to Technical Support Specialist / Level 2 in August 2022. I investigated customer configurations and failures, consulted existing knowledge, and worked with senior triage staff and Development on issues requiring further investigation. I supported cloud and on-premise environments across SOTI ONE. As an aligned engineer for enterprise customers, I maintained continuity on complex issues, helped Level 1 colleagues with escalations, and achieved an overall NPS of 94.

title: 2.3 Knowledge work within Support
text: As a key member of Project Sherpa, I identified knowledge gaps and authored more than 60 knowledge-base articles across SOTI Identity, SOTI Connect, SOTI XSight, and SOTI MobiControl. These articles had over 140 case attachments and some of the highest internal view counts. I helped agents structure and format articles, shared documentation practices with managers and team leads, verified technical details with Product Management and SMEs, and tracked North American deliverables. In January 2024, I supported a regional goal of one knowledge-base article per agent each week and gathered closed-case data to help track progress. This is the clearest connection between the support and writing chapters of my career. I was already translating technical findings into reusable material and helping others communicate it consistently before entering a formal writing role.

title: 2.4 Moving into Technical Writing
text: My transition into writing began with an internal development opportunity in March 2024, followed by the formal Technical Writer I role from April 2024 through February 2026. Early contributions included onboarding guidance for profile attributes and conditions in Oxygen XML and helping establish a dedicated environment for technical writers. As a Technical Writer I, I used DITA/XML, Oxygen, Git, WebHelp/HTML5, and CSS to plan and deliver user guides, SDK documentation, and integration manuals. I worked with Product Management, Development, and QA, incorporated review feedback, and used ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot to assist drafting and review. This was end-to-end product documentation work: deciding what a release changed for readers, drafting or revising the affected material, resolving technical questions with the product team, and taking changes through review into the help. Chapter 5 follows that process into named examples and inspectable writing changes. The change in role shifted my main output from customer cases and knowledge articles to product help, topic sets, and release-related documentation. The technical investigation remained relevant: a procedure still required an accurate understanding of how the feature worked and the conditions under which the reader would use it.

title: 2.5 Technical Writer II
text: I became Technical Writer II in March 2026. As a senior technical writer on the team, I lead online help deliverables for SOTI MobiControl, the company's flagship product, and help facilitate team initiatives and projects. I improve templates and workflows, produce and analyze monthly departmental metrics, support colleagues, and apply troubleshooting experience to documentation accuracy. The 2026 examples show that scope through feature research, migration validation, Umbraco workflow design, content-integrity proposals, documentation utilities, AI workflows, and shared-repository work. These activities align with the wider research, collaboration, and systems responsibilities of my senior writing role. In this senior writing role, leading a documentation effort also means improving the way the team produces and checks content. The AI workflow, review method, migration tooling, and quality checks make that expanded responsibility concrete through practical examples. Across the timeline, support, research, writing, and knowledge transfer remain visible. What expands is the range of things I work on: from customer systems and articles, to product topic sets, and then to the authoring, migration, review, and automation systems around the content.

title: 2.6 AI workflows in my senior writing role
text: In my senior role as a Technical Writer II, I began improving the system around documentation as well as the topics themselves. An AI-assisted authoring workflow brings Jira issues, design mockups, existing help, and source validation together to give writers a reviewable starting draft. A peer-review skill captures patterns from approximately 2,500 peer-review comments I mined from Git history, then uses those patterns as guidance for future reviews. The same approach extends to migration tooling, Figma retrieval, and documentation quality checks. I use AI to accelerate research, conversion, and inspection while retaining human review of product facts, editorial decisions, and published content. The linked projects explain the tools and processes I developed.

title: 3.1 Investigating SOTI MobiControl problems
text: I start troubleshooting by gathering relevant details and identifying possible points of failure. I research documentation and related cases in SharePoint, SOTI Wiki, SOTI Help, and Salesforce, then use logs and diagnostics to narrow the investigation. For unexpected behavior or possible defects, I work with senior specialists, SMEs, and triage leads and document issues in Jira for Development. I use Android ADB and dump-state information, server Event Viewer output, application logs, and SQL Server Management Studio to investigate issues. My database work includes queries, table checks, and maintenance operations in the relevant support context. For cloud environments, I monitored virtual-machine resources, firewall configuration, and application-specific upgrades. My SOTI MobiControl support responsibilities included environment setup, cloud/server upgrades and maintenance, and cloning customer environments for investigation.

title: 3.2 SOTI MobiControl device management across platforms
text: Within SOTI MobiControl support, I worked with Windows CE and Windows Desktop Classic and Modern enrollment and configuration. My Apple work covered iOS and macOS, Apple Business Manager, automated enrollment, volume-purchase application deployment, and configuration settings. On Android, I supported enterprise, BYOD, Corporate Personal, and Classic mobility implementations. The supporting ecosystem includes Honeywell Enterprise Provisioner, Zebra StageNow, Samsung Knox, and Apple Business Manager. I also set up and troubleshot SOTI Cloud Link Agents for on-premise directory-service integration. This platform-specific experience provides context for the later writing examples on enrollment and device configuration, without implying that I independently designed each underlying platform capability.

title: 3.3 SOTI Connect, SOTI XSight, and SOTI Identity
text: I also supported SOTI Connect, SOTI XSight, and SOTI Identity. For SOTI Connect, I installed and configured environments using MQTT and REST protocol adapters and HiveMQ brokers, and configured Zebra and SATO mobile printers. For SOTI XSight, I diagnosed remote-control and operational-data issues. For SOTI Identity, I configured roles and permissions and integrated identity providers and directory services with Azure Active Directory, now Microsoft Entra ID. This breadth extends beyond terminology about a single product. I worked with devices, protocols, access control, directory integration, and diagnostics; the Skills page connects those areas to specific roles and tasks. The Skills page pairs each product and supporting tool with the role in which I used it. The writing chapter then shows how that product understanding informed later help research and revisions.

title: 3.4 Customer continuity and colleague support
text: As an aligned engineer, I built familiarity with each customer's cloud or on-premise environment and ongoing concerns. I helped junior agents handle escalations and provided feedback, while turning recurring support questions into reusable knowledge-base guidance.

title: 4.2 Custom DITA and XML Authoring Tool
text: Oxygen licensing limited who could work directly with structured documentation. I developed a custom DITA and XML authoring tool as a stopgap for authoring and review, and team managers used the runnable package while broader authoring options were explored. The practical problem was access: writers and reviewers needed to work with XML/DITA content without always having the same licensed authoring software. The package offered a useful interim route for that work. I used AI-assisted development to build the tool, translating an authoring need into a runnable utility used by my team.

title: 4.3 AI Documentation Authoring Workflow
text: The AI Help workflow addresses the amount of context a writer must gather before drafting a feature update. My workflow connects the Jira feature with comments, attachments, related issues, design evidence, and the existing help source. It then identifies affected topics, prepares changes, and runs review and validation checks. I used this process to prepare a complete AI-generated starting version of the SOTI MobiControl 2027.0 online help so other writers could work from a comparable draft instead of a blank page; each writer retained responsibility for the final content. The reusable element is the captured process. The training guide shared on July 3, 2026 describes setup, repository synchronization, invoking the skill with a Jira identifier, impact analysis, file and TOC changes, and validation. It was written for two colleagues so the method could be transferred to other writers. The reusable Jira and peer-review downloads let other writers adapt parts of this approach to their own products and documentation systems.

title: 4.4 Peer reviewing with AI
text: The peer-review project captures recurring editorial judgement in a reusable skill. I mined approximately 2,500 peer-review comments from Git commit history to identify recurring patterns, then refined the skill against differences between automated suggestions and my final edits. A 40-commit sample helped me test that feedback. The detailed guidance includes grammar, direct topic openings, UI terminology, wintitle and uicontrol treatment, and comment-only Oxygen-style review. The skill helps writers and reviewers apply consistent editorial standards to structured help content, with human judgement guiding the final changes. I refined the approach through repeated peer reviews of enrollment guidance, installer instructions, and other help topics. I incorporated grammar checks and feedback from my final edits into the reusable review guidance. I have also prepared a separate technical-docs peer review skill for other writers to customize. Its company-neutral checks preserve the useful workflow—verify the claim, inspect the reader route, then give concrete editorial feedback—without exporting the original review examples or internal paths. DITA and Oxygen guidance is optional within that copy. The download page explains its scope and installation.

title: 4.5 Umbraco Migration Tooling
text: The team wanted to move structured help from Oxygen XML into Umbraco so more contributors could participate without the same authoring licence. Manual re-entry was too slow for that scale. I developed AI-assisted conversion, reconciliation, and export workflows to carry existing content into Umbraco-compatible HTML and then into a static help package. The work had to preserve notes and tips, tables and merged cells, images and icons, local links, context-help identifiers, navigation, and search. I also worked on a graphical Umbraco Publishing Tool and product/version configuration as the input pipeline evolved. The migration process combines content conversion with checks on the resulting pages, links, media, and navigation. The engineering chapter explains the export requirements and validation approach.

title: 4.6 Figma Retrieval and Export
text: The Jira/Figma tool grew from a repeated need to locate design evidence associated with a feature. I designed it around Jira epics, Figma links across related tickets, multiple frames or images, image export, and a local browser interface. I also examined Figma account/API limits and the case for a Dev seat. Bringing related mockups together helps writers understand a feature without tracing every linked issue individually. The workflow accounts for designs with multiple frames and the access needed to retrieve them.

title: 4.7 Documentation Quality and Validation
text: The problem began with defects that were difficult to repair without a reliable inventory: broken links, missing or misdirected images, table rendering issues, and differences introduced by migration. I used AI-assisted checks and structured trackers to identify affected pages, record symptoms, and give reviewers a reproducible route to each issue. The broader quality chapter explains the validation practice. The Writing collection shows selected before-and-after examples of documentation improvements.

title: 4.8 Editorial Workflow and Content Integrity
text: As more people contribute to documentation, a review process needs clear ownership and a way to prevent one person's stale browser session from overwriting another's changes. I documented the editorial review path, circulated the workflow, proposed safeguards for content integrity in Umbraco, and reported a related defect. The operations chapter explains the review process and my proposed safeguards against overwriting another contributor’s changes.

title: 4.9 Reusable Jira Issue Workflow
text: I developed Jira and peer-review workflows to make technical knowledge and editorial judgement reusable. The downloadable skills are generic adaptations that others can install and customize for their own teams. The Jira issue workflow ZIP includes an installable skill, a portable PowerShell helper, and an example configuration. It can search, read, and create a requested issue, then retrieve it for confirmation. Follow the setup guide to configure your own Jira site, authentication, and REST API v2 connection.

title: 4.10 Reusable Documentation Peer Review
text: The technical-docs peer review ZIP includes an installable skill and focused guidance for reviewing product claims, reader flow, links, publishing risks, and language. It includes optional DITA and Oxygen guidance. Teams can customize the references for their own style guide and publishing system. These downloads let visitors try and adapt the methods described in the projects. Both packages use generic examples and require users to supply their own configuration.

title: 4.11 Project files and related work
text: The project files include two reusable Agent Skills with installation guidance for Codex and Claude. Explore the Writing examples for rendered comparisons and online help improvements.

title: 5. Technical writing and online help improvements
text: This chapter follows a single writing process from research and scoping through release work to improvements a reader can see in the help. The early examples establish what I investigated and what a topic needed to answer; the later comparison shows how guidance, structure, and coverage changed. Where the record shows a team-wide change rather than my individual commit, that attribution remains explicit.

title: 5.1 Establishing the documentation scope
text: My product-writing work involves determining what changed, what users need to understand, and which topics need updating. I use Jira requirements, product and test environments, design material, and SME discussions to define scope and resolve uncertainty. The examples below show how that research shapes the guidance I prepare. The interface-update review shows the value of that scoping work. In August 2024, I reviewed a new SOTI MobiControl interface with a product colleague, identified the affected topics, and described a smaller set of targeted changes instead of the larger reorganization originally anticipated. For a reader unfamiliar with the product, this meant updating the instructions where the interface had changed instead of reorganizing unrelated help.

title: 5.2 Signal properties conditions and events
text: While researching Signal documentation, I requested complete inventories of Signal properties, supported device families, system components, configurations, and events. Signal helps administrators monitor device conditions and act on them; incomplete lists would leave readers unsure which inputs and events the feature actually supports. My documentation improvement was to seek the missing scope before writing or revising guidance. This research supported my understanding of Signal, which helps administrators monitor device conditions and act on them. Across the team, the help evolved into a wizard-oriented structure covering conditions, actions, schedules, properties, events, examples, upgrades, services, troubleshooting, and macros.

title: 5.3 Device audit logging
text: For Device Audit Logging, I investigated design material and sought clarification on the location and composition of generated device logs. Readers need to know where diagnostic records appear and what each log contains; an inaccurate location would make a troubleshooting procedure unusable. When the available information was uncertain, I pursued another SME rather than relying on an unverified interpretation. The work included two SME conversations in February 2026. This example connects support-style investigation with writing: I identified the questions the guidance needed to answer. The certificate-deployment before-and-after shows a separate, directly inspectable example of turning technical detail into a guided procedure.

title: 5.4 Declarative and reactive application policies
text: I sought SME clarification on how declarative and reactive app policies differ, including update behaviour, managed application configuration, connectivity conditions, retry behaviour, and activation predicates. I then checked a draft with the SME. I discussed the draft with an SME in February 2026. These distinctions affect how administrators interpret an application policy. Clarifying the behavior helps writers explain the appropriate workflow and organize guidance by platform.

title: 5.5 Apple enrollment documentation
text: I reworked the Apple enrollment overview to clarify the differences between enrollment methods and added a capability matrix to help administrators compare their options. I also added dedicated guidance for account-driven device enrollment on iOS. The reader-facing Apple help comparison shows the broader reorganization, while the Apple enrollment before-and-after isolates a specific committed overview change. These views answer different questions: how the section evolved, and what one selected revision actually changed. Across the team, Apple enrollment help was reorganized around device-based, user-based, and account-driven enrollment. The structure also clarified macOS and tvOS guidance, Apple Business Manager terminology, and supporting policy-management tasks.

title: 5.6 Additional feature research
text: My additional investigations covered Microsoft outbound email and Office 365 SMTP, feature scope and designs, and the move of Enterprise Apps from Policies/App Policies into Device Resources. I also worked on documentation updates with review constraints, comparisons between draft and mainline help, feature and device-support research, and a runtime note for release 2026.1.2 and later. Additional exploratory work included eSIM-related research and Signal documentation research.

title: 5.7 Release procedures and structured delivery
text: I follow a structured release process: assess and prioritize the request, research the feature, draft the guidance, obtain SME and peer review, publish, and communicate completion. I use requirements, QA test plans, SME interviews, and sprint demonstrations to check that the help reflects the intended behavior. I contributed an earlier version of the release-note procedure with a colleague. The described process uses a Jira request, a shared Word draft, Technical Writer review, manager peer review, and the subsequent publishing workflow. The procedure later evolved, so I retain my contribution without claiming authorship of every part of its current version. The following sections show the reader-facing result of that writing work, with the Writing collection providing exact before-and-after source pairs.

Repository synchronization and validation keep generated content compatible with the publishing system. The AI authoring project account explains this release-help workflow.

text: I mined approximately 2,500 peer-review comments from Git commit history to shape this skill's review guidance. I refined it when an automated review missed something I subsequently corrected. The project account explains the reusable skill. The skill makes recurring editorial decisions easier to explain, apply, and refine through human review.

The integrations also include Figma design retrieval, API/export investigations, and packaging workflows for different AI environments. title: 6.6 Refining workflows through practice

title: 7. Documentation engineering and automation
text: This chapter develops the engineering detail behind Umbraco migration tooling, Figma retrieval, and documentation validation. The Writing examples show how source changes can be inspected in a rendered form.

title: 7.1 Preserving content through migration
text: I investigated how to preserve content structure, authoring behavior, rendered output, and publication packaging during migration. I compared HTML, DITA, Markdown, and hybrid approaches, checked output against existing SOTI XSight help, and worked on static packages compatible with Pulse/WebHelp. My checks cover notes and tips, title spacing, table widths and merged cells, image dimensions, icons, media folders, static assets, links, context help, search, and on-page navigation. I also examined how task sections such as About this task and Procedure translate into the target authoring model. These details explain why migration is more than transferring prose. The structure and relationships must survive, and the rendered result must still function as help. The quality chapter retains the observations that informed this work.

title: 7.2 Export configuration and publishing tools
text: I worked on build-numbered export folders and product/version-specific configurations to support multiple help releases. I shaped a publishing-tool interface for technical writers, with configurable access, export options, progress feedback, and a simpler page layout. The interface makes a technically involved export easier for a writer to configure, run, and check. My investigations included test-content cleanup, locating source HTML, reconciling SOTI Identity imports, comparing exporter packages, and inspecting current files.

title: 7.3 Structured content transformations
text: I investigated table-formatting limitations in the DITA-OT Markdown pipeline and proposed three approaches: testing the markdown_github output, adding a lightweight Python post-processor, and considering a custom XSLT plugin for longer-term support. I developed a Windows/Python utility and guide for finding images outside DITA figure elements. The tool follows map and topic references, offers a size filter and scan-only mode, and exports reports. Its desktop interface uses Tkinter and Python’s standard library. I used nested and merged-table inventories to identify structures needing special attention during conversion and to guide transformation checks.

title: 7.4 Human readable review interfaces
text: I explored rendered HTML comparisons so reviewers could inspect DITA changes without reading XML. The approach uses full-page previews, highlighted differences, and before-and-after views. The ten writing comparisons demonstrate this review approach on selected examples. I explored an SME review interface with rendered content, comments, and possible visual editing to make technical review more accessible to colleagues. Other review-related investigations counted ditamap-linked topics with substep elements, located file references and author history, and divided linked SOTI MobiControl 2026.1 topics among reviewers. These supporting utilities help define review scope and assignment but are not interchangeable with the authoring substitute tool.

title: 7.5 Jira Figma and reporting integrations
text: I developed the Figma retrieval workflow around a recurring research problem: designs were spread across child and linked Jira issues. I worked on discovering relevant mockups, handling multiple frames, exporting images, and presenting them in a local browser interface. My reporting experiments include a refreshable Aha workbook for the Technical Writing team, Excel/Jira Data Center guidance, ticket-status notifications, and commit-history analysis. I used an exported pivot as the starting point for a more useful refreshable view.

title: 8. Documentation quality and validation
text: The Documentation Quality and Validation project tells the problem-and-response story. This chapter retains the underlying checks, inventories, and limits; the Writing collection shows selected changes where a source revision can be inspected directly.

title: 8.1 Making quality issues actionable
text: My quality work covers structured content, transformed output, web rendering, links, media, and editorial conventions. I turn defects into clear observations that another writer or engineer can reproduce and investigate. I created and maintained trackers for broken images, broken links across releases, rendering defects, nested and merged tables, migration discrepancies, and recurring peer-review lessons. Each gives the team a practical starting point for investigation or improvement.

title: 8.2 Migration and rendered output checks
text: I participated in a team comparison of Pulse-dev and live SOTI XSight content. We examined table titles, inline images, image sizes, anchors, step formatting, notes, and code presentation, and recorded issues in an authoring-tool feedback workbook. My migration investigations also include content notes that did not appear in the expected block model, malformed rendered tables, table titles and line breaks, and preservation of image scale. Keeping the exact symptoms matters because “formatting problem” alone does not supply enough information for another person to reproduce a defect.

title: 8.3 Editorial judgement and review practice
text: I refine review guidance by comparing automated suggestions with my final edits, including UI terminology, grammar, and direct topic openings. I retain the reason for each change so the lesson can inform future reviews. A generalized peer-review skill is available to adapt. I also investigated system-requirements feedback and combined help best practices. In one storage-space example, wording ranged from 300 MB to unlimited space; I worked to make that explanation more actionable for readers.

title: 8.4 Quality checks and follow-through
text: One cross-version quality inventory documented 23 observations across 21 affected topics. Another identified 31 image-link failures across 22 topics and 13 distinct image URLs. These inventories helped turn scattered output problems into specific items for investigation. My broader help review covered 474 area/page entries across 466 distinct file paths and identified 45 candidates for conversion into clearer task guidance. I also checked the availability of 219 help URLs. These inventories supported scoping and follow-up alongside individual writing improvements. My quality work combines inventories, review activity, and defect reporting. The writing examples connect selected findings to visible source changes and validation context.

title: 9. Workflows and documentation operations
text: The Editorial Workflow and Content Integrity project summarizes the problem. The sections here retain the review path, stale-editor scenario, proposed safeguards, and reporting context behind it.

title: 9.1 Editorial ownership in Umbraco
text: In May 2026, I reviewed initial Umbraco workflow requirements and reframed them into two clearer scenarios: content authored by a Technical Writer/Senior Technical Writer, and content authored by an approved Technical Support agent. My version distinguished formal reviewers from general commenters and clarified drafting, SME validation, peer review, ownership, permissions, and publication to dev. The workflow was forwarded as the current documentation-production workflow to be replicated in the Umbraco Workflow plugin. Production publication remained a separate Web-team responsibility. That boundary matters: publication to dev within the editorial workflow is not the same as authority to deploy the production website.

title: 9.2 Stale editor overwrite prevention
text: Testing in June exposed a content-integrity problem involving two writers opening the same topic. One could enter Workflow Drafting while the other retained an older browser copy, creating a possible later overwrite. I documented the scenario and proposed a claim/unclaim safeguard independent of workflow stages. I proposed safeguards covering editorial ownership, save-time checks on the server, workflow integration, and permissions for overriding or reassigning a lock. A server-side check would address stale browser sessions before they could overwrite newer changes. After discussing the behavior with the Web team, I submitted a workflow-plugin bug report describing the overwrite risk and the proposed save-time safeguards.

title: 9.3 Process documentation and communication
text: My contributions span the writing process: scoping requests, checking product facts, documenting release-note procedures, recording migration problems, and clarifying editorial ownership. I explored clearer documentation-status notifications for Product Managers who were missing updates among other Jira messages. I proposed a Power Automate approach and discussed its suitability with IT.

title: 9.4 Reporting and measurement
